title: From free speech advocates to critics: The Trump administration’s new rhetoric promotes support for censorship among Trump voters
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
one_line: A preregistered survey experiment with 13,305 quota-matched US adults (October 2025) tested how exposure to real anti-speech quotes from Trump and his allies, following Charlie Kirk's assassination, shifted support for government censorship of the out-party.
key_claims: Trump voters exposed to the explicit anti-speech rhetoric significantly increased support for government censorship of out-party media and individuals (β = 0.35, described as roughly one in three respondents shifting toward neutrality or acceptance).
Non-Trump voters (Harris voters, third-party voters, non-voters) showed a backlash effect, becoming significantly more protective of out-party speech after the same exposure.
Effects were equivalent whether quotes were attributed to Trump/allies by name or to a generic 'prominent politician' — no statistically significant interaction with attribution.
Researcher-generated pro-speech quotes matched in style produced no significant effect in either group, suggesting norm violation rather than norm confirmation drives attitude change.
Authors frame the shift as 'democratic neutrality' — norm erosion via people ceasing to actively defend the norm rather than embracing authoritarianism.
limitations: Captures a short-term attitudinal snapshot; whether repeated exposure produces durable opinion change is untested (authors' stated caveat).
Outcome is self-reported survey attitudes, not measured behaviour; real-world examples cited (Jimmy Kimmel suspension, employee terminations) are contextual, not experimental outcomes.
Single-country, single-moment design tied to one unusual triggering event, limiting generalisation to other elites or norms.
Control condition pro-speech quotes were researcher-generated rather than real elite statements, so stimuli were not fully matched in authenticity.
open_questions: Does sustained, repeated exposure to anti-speech elite rhetoric consolidate the observed shift into durable attitude change, or does it decay within news cycles?
Do the measured attitude shifts predict actual behaviour, such as supporting or tolerating concrete censorship actions?
Would the same rhetoric from an out-party elite produce mirror-image effects, testing whether the mechanism is partisan cue-taking rather than content?
